facts: Muncaster Castle has been owned by the Pennington family for over 800 years.
It sits at the western edge of the Lake District, overlooking the Esk estuary.
Ravenglass is the only coastal village within the Lake District National Park.
Sellafield was originally a Second World War munitions factory before becoming a nuclear site in the 1940s.
It is one of the largest nuclear sites in Europe and remains a major local employer.
The station was built specifically to serve the site's workforce.
Carlisle Castle has stood for over 900 years and was fought over repeatedly during centuries of border conflict with Scotland.
Mary, Queen of Scots was briefly held there in 1568.
Carlisle is the largest settlement in Cumbria and the network's main hub.
Windermere is England's largest natural lake, around 18km long.
The station is not actually in the town of Bowness-on-Windermere itself, a common source of confusion for visitors.
The branch line to Windermere opened in 1847, built to bring Victorian tourists to the Lakes.
Robert Burns spent the last years of his life in Dumfries and is buried in the town.
Dumfries is sometimes called the 'Queen of the South', also the name of its football club.
The town sits on the Glasgow South Western Line, on the cross-border route toward Carlisle.

landmark: The Old Blacksmith's Shop, Gretna Green
facts: Gretna Green became famous for runaway weddings after a 1754 law tightened marriage rules in England but not Scotland.
It sits just north of the border, the first village travellers reach entering Scotland this way.
The village still holds thousands of weddings a year.
Appleby (Appleby-in-Westmorland) was historically the county town of Westmorland.
The castle's keep dates back to the 12th century.
The town is also famous for its annual Horse Fair, one of Europe's largest Traveller gatherings.
St Bees Head is the only stretch of Heritage Coast between Wales and Scotland on England's west coast.
It's the official starting point of Wainwright's Coast to Coast walk.
The cliffs host England's only mainland colony of black guillemots.
Furness Abbey was once one of the wealthiest monasteries in England before its dissolution in 1537.
Its red sandstone ruins sit in a wooded valley known as the 'Vale of Deadly Nightshade'.
Barrow-in-Furness grew rapidly in the 19th century around shipbuilding and steel.
